note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Young female presents with 2 days of lower abdominal (suprapubic) pain with mild nausea, sensations of being hot/sweaty, and increased urinary frequency; reports slight pink discoloration of urine.
- Clinician assessed likely urinary tract infection, arranged a short course oral antibiotic to be sent to patient's allocated pharmacy and advised return for worsening symptoms or failure to improve.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Suspected urinary tract infection (UTI) / lower urinary tract symptoms
- Presentation: 2 days of lower central abdominal (suprapubic) pain described as needle-like; associated mild nausea (no vomiting), feeling hot and sweaty, increased thirst, and slightly increased urinary frequency.
- Urine symptom detail: patient reports slight pink discoloration of urine; denies pain on passing urine and denies foul smell.
- Bowel and systemic: recent constipation last week that has resolved; no diarrhoea; no vomiting; no back pain or flank pain.
- Vital sign: measured oral/other temperature ~37°C one hour prior (no documented fever above 37°C).
- Gynecologic: regular periods; no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding; no vaginal discharge reported.
- Examination: no physical examination documented.
- Differential/assessment: clinician’s impression — likely urinary tract infection.
- Management provided: clinician advised and will send a short course oral antibiotic (twice daily for 3 days) to patient’s allocated pharmacy; patient agreed to treatment.
- Safety netting: advised to contact service or seek face-to-face assessment if pain worsens, high temperature develops, back pain develops, new symptoms occur, or if recurrent episodes happen.

Issue 2:
- No other active problems raised during this consult.

Issue 3:
- No other active problems raised during this consult.

Medications:
- No regular prescription medications reported.
- Proposed: oral antibiotic — agent not documented; prescribed twice daily for 3 days (dose/route/frequency details limited to "twice daily for 3 days").

Allergies:
- Amoxycillin.

Past Medical History:
- Patient reports no significant past medical history aside from routine minor illnesses (colds, flu).
- Family history: mother had breast cancer treated/cured.

Social History:
- Lives with parents.
- Alcohol: approximately one beer per drinking occasion, about 4 times per week.
- Tobacco: denies smoking.
- Sexual/reproductive: history of an internal contraceptive implant for one year — current status unclear (see conflicts).

Preventative History:
- No explicit details provided about cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, recent optometry, or skin checks.

Physical Examination:
- No physical examination findings documented.
- Vitals: single temperature measurement ~37°C (measured ~1 hour before consult). No other vital signs documented.

Plan:
- Send oral antibiotic prescription to the patient’s allocated pharmacy; patient to start immediately upon receipt (twice daily for 3 days as advised).
- Advise patient to contact service or present for face-to-face assessment if:
  - Increasing abdominal pain,
  - Development of high temperature,
  - New back/flank pain,
  - New or worsening urinary symptoms,
  - Recurrence of the same problem.
- If symptoms fail to improve or worsen, arrange in-person review for examination and further investigations (urinalysis, urine culture, pregnancy test if indicated).
- No additional investigations or referrals were documented in this consult.

document_quality (Quality checks):
- Missing but clinically expected elements: pregnancy status or pregnancy test (patient of reproductive age); urine dipstick/urine culture results; specific antibiotic agent name, dose, and route details beyond "twice daily"; other vital signs; physical examination findings.
- Internal conflicts: patient statement about internal contraceptive implant is ambiguous — reported having had an implant for one year and also stated "no more" (status in situ unclear).
- Transcript quality: mostly intelligible with occasional interruptions and incomplete phrases; no critical audio gaps preventing clinical interpretation.
